newsitem.title: USA: Alleged gang members to stand trial in Ngor murder.
newsitem.headline: Alleged gang members to stand trial in Ngor murder.

text.p: Three suspected gang members were ordered on Thursday to stand trial for the murder of Oscar-winning Cambodian actor Haing Ngor.

"It's an outrage," defence lawyer Kenneth Kahn shouted in court as Judge Stephen Marcus ordered the suspects held without bail. The defence lawyer alleges the three were framed by police and that Ngor was probably the victim of a political assassination.
Marcus set an Oct. 24 date for formal arraignment on felony murder and robbery charges. Indra Lim, Jason Chan and Tak Sun Tan, all 19, are allegedly members of the "Asian Lazy Boys" street gang.
As the three were being led away in handcuffs, Kahn shouted to them: "You guys have been framed."
Later outside the court he compared the case to last year's O.J. Simpson murder trial, in which the defence alleged the ex-American football star was framed by Los Angeles police.
"The O.J. Simpson case was like child's play compared to what they did in this case," Kahn told reporters.
Assistant Attorney General Craig Hum characterised Kahn's allegations of police misconduct as "not worthy of comment" and said the assassination theory was groundless.
"There's nothing, not a bit of evidence to show this was anything more than a street robbery," Hum told reporters.

Ngor, 55, who won the best supporting actor Oscar for "The Killing Fields" in 1984, was shot and killed on Feb. 25 in the driveway of his home in the Chinatown section of Los Angeles. The film chronicled the genocidal regime of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, which the actor denounced vociferously.
During the preliminary hearing, Kahn told Judge Marcus that there was no physical evidence, such as fingerprints, footprints or a weapon linking the suspects to the murder.
Kahn raised the theory that Ngor was assassinated because of his outspoken criticism of human rights in Cambodia.
Ngor, he said, "is not your ordinary, average citizen."

Pointing out that police found only two spent cartridges at the scene of the crime, Kahn said: "Is it more consistent with the theory of robbery or is it more consistent with a political 'hit' for the purpose of silencing somebody?"

He said the killing was "a well-oiled, well-executed plan," and he questioned why police had not tried harder to trace a grey car with tinted windows seen pulling away from an alleyway close to Ngor's home the night of the killing.

The defence also pointed out that one witness who first told the court he had seen the three suspects running from the vicinity of the murder at the time later recanted his testimony and said he had been told what to say by police.

In his argument in court, Hum acknowledged police might have conducted better interrogation of the witness who recanted. He said, however "that doesn't make it coerced and it certainly doesn't make it a lie.
"They're (defense) going to attack the police, they're gonna' put the police on trial," said Hum, who added that the fact that Ngor's watch was taken was a sign it was a robbery.
